british: a comprehensive on the edge of town with a famously muddy playing field
whose Victorian bell tower still rings for the end of lunch
where the head teacher knows every pupil by name
rated outstanding, though nobody quite remembers why
where the school play is the highlight of the year
with a canteen famous for its chips and its jam roly-poly
whose netball team has not lost a match in six years
housed in a red-brick building that used to be a workhouse
where the Year 11 prom is the talk of the town
with a leaky science block and a brilliant chemistry teacher
whose old boys and girls include a famous children’s author
where the school dog wanders the corridors at break
that merged with its rival across the river last summer
with a library that stays open until six for anyone who needs it
where the sixth-form common room has a temperamental kettle
whose choir once sang on the radio
set beside the canal, with geese on the football pitch
where every Friday ends with a whole-school assembly
with a vegetable garden run by the eco-club
whose uniform is a famously bright shade of purple
where the caretaker has worked for forty years
american: with a football stadium bigger than the town hall
where the homecoming parade shuts Main Street every October
whose marching band has won the state title three years running
where everyone hangs out in the parking lot after class
with a school paper that has broken more than one local scandal
where the senior prank is a sacred tradition
whose science fair winners went on to work for NASA
with a rivalry against the school across the river that goes back a century
where the cafeteria serves pizza every Friday
with lockers that jam if you look at them wrong
where the drama club puts on a musical every spring
whose basketball team plays to a packed gym every Friday night
where the class of ’99 buried a time capsule under the flagpole
with a principal who greets every student at the door
boarding: a rambling country house with a lake and its own chapel
where the houses compete fiercely for the end-of-year cup
whose dormitories are said to be haunted by a friendly ghost
where midnight feasts are strictly forbidden and frequently held
set on a windswept clifftop overlooking the sea
with a secret tunnel that every pupil knows about and no teacher admits to
founded in 1592 by a wool merchant’s widow
where the lacrosse team is feared across three counties
with an ivy-covered library and a resident owl
where new pupils must find their way out of the maze on their first day
whose matron makes the best cocoa in England
where letters from home arrive every Thursday
with a crumbling observatory on the east tower
where the school founder’s portrait watches every exam
set in an old abbey deep in the moors
whose rowing eight has never beaten its rival upriver
where the end of term is marked by a bonfire on the hill
with a school farm, two donkeys and a very bad-tempered goat
where tuck boxes are guarded like treasure
whose motto is carved over the great oak door
anime: where the cherry trees along the front gate bloom on the first day of term
whose rooftop is officially off limits and never empty at lunch
famous for its cultural festival and its haunted music room
where the student council president is rumoured to be a genius
with a volleyball team that has not won in a decade
where every club fights for new members in April
perched on a hill above the sea, reached by a long flight of steps
whose school store sells out of melon bread within minutes
where the light music club practises in a disused classroom
with a clock tower that has stopped at 4:44
whose swimming pool is cleaned by whichever class loses a bet
where the transfer student arrived on a very windy morning
with a library that holds a diary nobody can explain
famous for its kendo club and its fierce student council
where students race the last train home after club practice
whose sports festival is the biggest event of the year
with a garden club that grows prize-winning sunflowers
where the school idol group performs on the steps every Friday
beside a shrine where students leave wishes before exams
where the summer training camp is held by the sea
fantasy: where squires train with wooden swords in the castle yard
whose students ride griffins to their morning lessons
where bards learn a thousand songs before they may leave
set inside the walls of a ruined fortress
where rangers learn to track a deer across bare stone
whose healers are welcome on every battlefield
built on a cliff where the young dragons nest
where every graduate is given a map with one corner left blank
founded by a retired adventuring party
whose archery butts stand among the apple orchards
where the final exam is a night alone in the old forest
with a hall of banners from every graduate’s first quest
run by an old knight with a wooden leg and a soft heart
where students learn to read seven alphabets
whose stables hold horses from every kingdom
set on an island reached only at low tide
where apprentices forge their first blade in their final year
whose library is guarded by a very old tortoise
where the duelling ring has stood for four hundred years
built in the branches of a great oak
